content: 1. The relationship between physical activity and the risk of endometrial cancer is not well-defined. 2. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis, conducted in accordance with the MOOSE guidelines, was to determine whether physical activity during youth and throughout life reduces the risks of breast cancer, colon cancer, and endometrial cancer. 3. Relevant observational studies published up to July 2018 were identified through searches in the PubMed and Web of Science databases. 4. Observational studies, including prospective cohort, case-cohort, nested case-control, historical cohort, and case-control designs, were included if they examined the association between physical activity (either during youth or over a lifetime) and the risk of developing breast, colon, or endometrial cancers. 5. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to calculate the summary relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the highest versus the lowest levels of physical activity of any type. 6. Eighty publications were included in the meta-analysis. 7. For breast cancer, menopausal status did not appear to influence the observed inverse association between physical activity and cancer risk. 8. The findings suggest that engaging in physical activity throughout life, starting from early childhood, may reduce the risks of developing breast cancer, colon cancer, and endometrial cancer. 9. Definitions, exclusions, and self-reported physical activity types were considered in the analysis. 10. The outcomes addressed included breast, colon, and endometrial cancers, and the populations analyzed were adults. 11. This study was supported by grants from the Suzhou Science and Technology Bureau (No. SYS201741). 12. Impaired sleep quality and quantity are associated with increased risks of future morbidity and mortality. 13. Exercise is a potential non-pharmacological intervention to improve sleep, but the effects of resistance exercise on sleep are not well understood. 14. A systematic review of the literature was conducted to evaluate the acute and chronic effects of resistance exercise on sleep quality and quantity. 15. Thirteen studies were included in the review. 16. Chronic resistance exercise was found to improve all aspects of sleep, with the greatest benefits observed in sleep quality. 17. However, the benefits of resistance exercise were diminished when combined with aerobic exercise compared to aerobic exercise alone. 18. The acute effects of resistance exercise on sleep remain poorly studied and inconsistent. 19. Resistance exercise training also improves anxiety and depression, suggesting it may be an effective intervention for enhancing sleep quality. 20. Further research is needed to better understand the acute effects of resistance exercise on sleep, the physiological mechanisms underlying sleep changes, and the impact of chronic resistance exercise on sleep architecture. 21. Future studies should also explore the timing and dose-response effects of exercise to determine the optimal prescription for sleep benefits. 22. Epidemiological evidence regarding the association between physical activity and lung cancer risk remains controversial. 23. A meta-analysis of cohort studies was conducted to evaluate the relationship between physical activity and lung cancer risk in men, women, and high-risk populations such as smokers. 24. Twenty cohort studies involving 2,965,811 participants and 31,807 lung cancer cases were included. 25. An inverse association was observed between physical activity and lung cancer risk. 26. Subgroup analyses stratified by smoking intensity and duration yielded similar relative risk magnitudes. 27. Increased physical activity may be associated with a lower risk of lung cancer, particularly among smokers rather than non-smokers. 28. Large interventional studies are needed to confirm these findings. 29. Programmed exercise interventions lasting at least six weeks were evaluated for their effects on mild-to-moderate anxiety symptoms in midlife and older women. 30. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to clarify the impact of exercise on anxiety symptoms in this population. 31. Randomized controlled trials comparing exercise interventions to no intervention were included. 32. Exercise interventions were classified as mid-term (12 weeks to 4 months) or long-term (6 to 14 months) and as low-intensity (e.g., walking, yoga) or moderate-intensity (e.g., aerobic exercise). 33. Mid-term exercise interventions of low-to-moderate intensity appeared to improve mild-to-moderate anxiety symptoms in midlife and older women. 34. Physical exercise is a promising intervention to prevent or delay cognitive decline in individuals aged 50 years and older. 35. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to determine the effectiveness of physical exercise in improving cognitive function in this population. 36. The review included randomized controlled trials of exercise interventions in community-dwelling adults aged 50 years or older, with cognitive function as an outcome measure. 37. Aerobic exercise, resistance training, multicomponent training, and Tai Chi all demonstrated significant benefits for cognitive function. 38. Exercise sessions lasting 45-60 minutes at moderate intensity were associated with cognitive benefits. 39. The results were consistent across cognitive domains and independent of participants' baseline cognitive status. 40. Physical exercise improved cognitive function in adults over 50, regardless of their cognitive status. 41. Clinicians are encouraged to recommend aerobic and resistance exercise of at least moderate intensity on as many days of the week as feasible, in line with current exercise guidelines. 42. Associations between leisure-time physical activity, low HDL cholesterol, and mortality were investigated in a pooled analysis of nine population-based cohorts in Britain. 43. Meeting physical activity guidelines was defined as engaging in at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity, 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity activity, or equivalent combinations. 44. There were 2,250 deaths during 326,016 person-years of follow-up. 45. Cardiovascular disease mortality hazard ratios were similar, although confidence intervals were wider. 46. No statistically significant evidence of biological interaction between physical inactivity and low HDL cholesterol was observed. 47. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to identify the association between physical activity domains (e.g., total, transport, household, occupational, leisure) and chronic diseases among South Asian adults aged 40 years or older. 48. Inactive or less active South Asian adults were found to have a 31% higher risk of being hypertensive.
